title: A home for my EMBA learning
summary: How materials become connected, reusable knowledge in this repository.
text:
## From material to knowledge

Share slides, a keyword, an article, a URL, or rough notes with the capture agent. Each input becomes a source-grounded Markdown note, assigned to a category and connected to relevant ideas.

This guide describes the learning system. It does not represent completed coursework.

## A useful note answers four questions

1. What is the central idea?
2. What evidence and assumptions support it?
3. Where could it be applied?
4. What remains unclear?

## Finding connections

Browse categories to explore a subject. Search titles, tags, course names, and note text to find a specific idea. Related notes connect frameworks across courses. A note has one primary category and can have several tags.

## Keeping the record honest

Source summaries and personal reflections stay distinct. Missing information is recorded as an open question. Keywords without context stay provisional until there is enough evidence to explain them.

## Adding the next learning

In this repository's Codex chat, say: “Capture this for my EMBA knowledge base,” and attach or paste the material. You can also specify a course, category, or business application. The repository instructions route the agent to the capture skill.

All authored documents are Markdown. Build and validation run locally before publishing the site. Draft notes are excluded from the site, but any file committed to this public repository is publicly accessible.

title: Geert Hofstede: understanding national culture
summary: Six dimensions for exploring cultural differences, with limits and questions for cross-border leadership.

sources.title: What is culture — definition and distinction from personality
The 6D model of national culture — dimensions explained and within-country variation
Levels of analysis — individuals, groups, and shared human attributes

text:
## Key takeaway

Hofstede's framework provides a vocabulary for exploring differences between societies. Use it to formulate questions about expectations, then investigate the actual team or business context. A country-level pattern does not establish how a particular person thinks or behaves.

The supplied website introduces Geert Hofstede (1928–2020), a Dutch social psychologist, and Gert Jan Hofstede's work. This note focuses on its national-culture framework. [Starting source](https://geerthofstede.com/).

## What culture means here

Culture refers to learned, shared expectations about social life. The site distinguishes this shared background from an individual's personality. Its focus includes everyday interactions, beyond culture in the artistic sense. [Source: What is culture](https://geerthofstede.com/culture-geert-hofstede-gert-jan-hofstede/definition-culture/).

## The six dimensions

These are brief paraphrases of the site's explanations, retaining its dimension names.

| Dimension | What it explores |
| --- | --- |
| Individualism / collectivism | Independence versus membership in interdependent social groups. |
| Power distance | Acceptance and expectation of unequal power by those with less power. |
| Masculinity / femininity | Social expectations around gender roles, toughness, winning, and sympathy for others; not an individual's sex or personality. |
| Uncertainty avoidance | Responses to ambiguity and the unknown; distinct from risk avoidance. |
| Long-term / short-term orientation | Adapting and preparing for change versus treating inherited traditions as a moral reference. |
| Indulgence / restraint | Freedom to enjoy life versus emphasis on duty and restriction. |

The website uses approximate 0–100 scales for comparison. It describes national maps as rough patterns with substantial variation within countries, and acknowledges that other dimensions can be constructed. [Source: 6D model, “Dimension maps” and “The dimensions explained”](https://geerthofstede.com/culture-geert-hofstede-gert-jan-hofstede/6d-model-of-national-culture/).

## Levels matter

The site's multilevel discussion distinguishes individuals, groups, and attributes shared by humans. **Learning implication:** do not substitute national averages for observation of individuals or an organization's working practices. [Source: Levels of analysis](https://geerthofstede.com/research-and-vsm/levels-of-analysis/).

## Application: a cross-border project team

*Hypothetical example and agent interpretation; not an experience supplied by the learner.*

A project manager notices that some colleagues challenge proposals openly while others raise concerns privately. Rather than assigning behavior to nationality, ask:

- Who is expected to make the decision, and how can people safely disagree?
- Which decisions need more explanation or predictability?
- What do people understand by individual ownership and collective responsibility?

Test practical changes: collect written concerns before meetings, clarify decision ownership, and agree how uncertainty will be communicated. Compare observed participation and delivery afterward. Treat culture as one possible explanation alongside role, incentives, language, and team history.

## My reflection

Awaiting learner input. No course, personal experience, or country comparison was supplied.

## Questions to revisit

- Which EMBA course or discussion does this connect to?
- What evidence would distinguish a cultural explanation from organizational incentives?
- How were the country scores sampled, and how current are the data?
- How do independent studies evaluate the model's validity?

## Connected idea and source scope

[Organizational culture](hofstede-organizational-culture.md) uses a separate framework about working practices. Its dimensions should not be confused with the national-culture dimensions.

Captured on 2026-10-04 from the linked website pages. This is an introductory source summary with labeled applications, not a review of the full research literature. Country scores, videos, and external comparison tools were not analyzed.

title: Hofstede: organizational culture as shared practices
summary: A separate framework for examining organizational practices, with important limits to its research base.

sources.title: 6 dimensions of organisational culture — project, dimensions, and limitations

text:
## Key takeaway

The site's organizational framework examines shared practices rather than the national-culture dimensions. The research found common understandings of practices even without shared values. [Source: “The organizational culture project”](https://geerthofstede.com/culture-geert-hofstede-gert-jan-hofstede/6-dimensions-organizational-culture/).

## Six practice dimensions

The source identifies these pairs:

- Process-oriented versus results-oriented.
- Job-oriented versus employee-oriented.
- Professional versus parochial.
- Open versus closed systems.
- Tight versus loose control.
- Pragmatic versus normative.

These are research descriptors, not a universal ranking of good and bad cultures.

## Evidence and limitations

The project studied 20 organizational units in Denmark and the Netherlands during the 1980s. The source cautions that this sample was not representative of all organizations and that applicability in different countries cannot be assumed. Industry and other organizational characteristics also matter. [Source: project scope and limitations](https://geerthofstede.com/culture-geert-hofstede-gert-jan-hofstede/6-dimensions-organizational-culture/).

## Application: compare stated values with daily work

*Hypothetical exercise and agent interpretation.*

A company says it values openness. Examine how a new employee actually gets information, asks questions, and raises a concern. Use concrete examples from onboarding and meetings before assigning a cultural label. Select one practice to improve and check whether the employee experience changes.

This exercise is a discussion prompt, not a validated culture survey or a scoring method.

## My reflection

Awaiting learner input.

## Questions to revisit

- Which repeated practices reinforce or contradict a team's stated values?
- How do industry, regulation, and job design affect those practices?
- What additional evidence supports applying this framework outside the original study?

## Connected idea and source scope

[National cultural dimensions](hofstede-cultural-dimensions.md) examine a different level of culture. Keep country-level comparisons and organization-level observations distinct.

Captured on 2026-10-04 as a companion to the learner's Hofstede website link. No company assessment or personal experience was supplied. Original research papers were not reviewed.
